extracted.intended_audience: academics and researchers (especially mathematicians), journal editors, and readers who follow scholarly publishing and retractions
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and practices around handling errors, errata, corrections, and retractions for published mathematics research papers, including editorial and peer-review responses. Focuses on when a paper should be corrected versus withdrawn and on transparency in that process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper was retracted because the proofs in the paper were found to be incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical papers must contain complete, correct proofs for their main results; incomplete proofs are a substantive defect that can render the results unreliable and justify withdrawal. Example/anti-pattern: publishing theorems whose proofs contain gaps that are discovered later when others attempt to use the techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author submission of erratum / corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may submit errata or corrections to address identified gaps or errors (author sent a one-page erratum, then expanded to two pages, later four pages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an error or gap is found, the author should prepare and submit an erratum/correction with sufficient detail. Corrections may be expanded in response to referee feedback to make the fix clearer for readers. Keep records of submissions and versions sent to the journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review of errata / referee scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Errata submitted to the journal can be sent to referees and themselves be subject to review; a referee found a new issue (an error in a lemma) in the submitted correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrections are not automatically accepted; they can trigger new referee review which may uncover further problems. Expect iterative revision and possible discovery of additional errors when errata are examined closely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction vs. correction decision criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: If it takes or will take numerous corrections to get it right then retraction is the only appropriate thing to do (comment: 'If it takes or will take numerous corrections to get it right then retraction is the only appropriate thing to do.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should weigh whether the errors are fixable by a single erratum or whether the extent/importance of the flaws means the published record is unreliable; widespread or deep errors may justify withdrawal rather than a series of incremental corrections. Alternative approaches (mega corrections) exist but may be less appropriate if the original is fundamentally compromised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial transparency and communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors requested referee reports and clarification but reported receiving little or delayed communication from the journal (journal acknowledged receipt of erratum but provided no further input for over a year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should acknowledge receipt of corrections, communicate status and reasoning for decisions (corrections vs withdrawal), and provide referee reports when requested; lack of transparency can leave authors confused and erode trust. Best practice: timely, clear feedback and sharing of referee reports related to correction/retraction decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community verification and reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Some mathematicians found a gap in one proof when they were trying to use the techniques, prompting the discovery of the issue years after publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validation by other researchers applying or extending results is an important corrective mechanism; ease of verification and clarity of arguments help the community detect and fix gaps. Papers should be written with sufficient detail for expert readers to reproduce and build on the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and small-expert-circle considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Delays in handling extremely technical corrections are not unusual given how technical papers in the journal can be and the expert circle is very, very small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals and authors should account for the reality that extremely specialized work may take longer to referee and verify, but reasonable timelines and updates on progress remain important. Long delays do not absolve the need for clear decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction notice content and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The retraction notice for the paper says only that the paper has been 'withdrawn' (notice lacked detail), while a spokesperson later explained the proofs were incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction/withdrawal notices ideally should state the reason for the action to inform the community; vague notices ('withdrawn') without explanation can leave ambiguity. Best practice: explicit, informative notices describing whether the issue was error, misconduct, or irreparable flaws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-retraction correction and dissemination options for authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Now that the paper has been withdrawn, the author plans to post his correction on arXiv.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction does not necessarily preclude the author from publicly posting corrected versions (e.g., on preprint servers) or later publishing a corrected manuscript; authors should use transparent public venues to share fixes and clarify the status of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction signals unreliability but allows future correction
rubrics_metrics.description: The retraction says that the original was incorrect and does not preclude the author from publishing a correct manuscript when and if they figure it out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A retraction serves to mark the published record as unreliable; it is not necessarily punitive but protective of the literature. It clarifies that findings should not be relied upon until corrected, while still allowing for republication of corrected, verified results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation counts and impact are not sole quality indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper has not yet been cited (according to Web of Science), but low citation counts in mathematics do not necessarily indicate correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citation metrics may reflect impact or visibility but are a poor proxy for correctness; assessment of reliability should focus on the soundness of proofs and community verification rather than citations alone.
